title: The Scanner as a Materials Problem
summary: Almost every design constraint in an MR scanner traces back to a material limit. The field is set by the critical surface of Nb-47wt%Ti, whose Tc of 9.2 K forces a 4.2 K liquid helium bath and everything that follows from it: cryostat, cold head, quench pipe and a helium supply chain the department does not control. The RF and gradient chains are a copper problem, where skin depth at the Larmor frequency puts all the current in the outer few microns and I-squared-R puts tens of kilowatts of heat into a water loop. Shielding is an iron and copper problem, which is why the room is a Faraday cage sitting inside tonnes of silicon steel.

facts.label: NbTi critical surface, and what sub-cooling buys
facts.value: Nb-47wt%Ti: Tc = 9.2 K at zero field, Bc2(0) = 14.5 T, falling to about 10.5 T at 4.2 K but rising to about 14 T at 1.8 K. Non-copper Jc above 3000 A/mm2 at 4.2 K and 5 T; engineering Jc of order 600 A/mm2 in a finished MRI conductor at the same point. The 11.75 T Iseult whole-body magnet is NbTi in 1.8 K pressurised superfluid helium at 1483 A, 308 H and 338 MJ in a 90 cm warm bore
facts.note: The critical surface is a surface: raising temperature or field lowers the current you can carry, so peak on-conductor field in a 4.2 K bath magnet is practically 8 to 9 T, which is what makes 7 T whole-body feasible in NbTi, and why the highest-field human magnet built to date reached 11.7 T by sub-cooling rather than by changing material.

facts.label: Nb3Sn, needed above roughly 10 T
facts.value: A15 Nb3Sn: Tc = 18.3 K, Bc2 above 24 T at 4.2 K (Bc20 quoted to about 30 T), whole-wire Jc of order 1000 A/mm2 at 4.2 K and 15 T. Reacted at 650 to 700 C for 100 to 200 h
facts.note: It is brittle: irreversible strain degradation sets in near 0.3 to 0.5 percent, so the coil is wound first and reacted afterwards (wind-and-react), which is why Nb3Sn appears as the inner-coil conductor of NMR magnets from about 14 T (600 MHz) upward, carries them to the all-low-temperature-superconductor ceiling near 23.5 T (1 GHz) where HTS inserts take over, and has never displaced NbTi in clinical MRI.

facts.label: Copper stabiliser and wire architecture
facts.value: Cu to superconductor ratio 1.3:1 to 2.5:1; OFHC copper with RRR above 100, so resistivity near 4 K is of order 1.7e-10 ohm m. MRI wire is typically 0.5 to 1.8 mm across with tens to a few hundred twisted NbTi filaments of 40 to 130 um
facts.note: The copper is not there to carry current in normal operation, it is there to carry it for the milliseconds after a filament goes normal and to conduct that heat away; more copper means better quench protection and lower engineering Jc, which is the whole design trade.

facts.label: Clinical magnet electrical parameters
facts.value: A 1.5 T whole-body magnet runs at roughly 250 to 500 A with 50 to 90 H inductance and 2 to 6 MJ stored energy; a 3 T magnet is roughly double the stored energy. Persistent-mode drift of 0.1 ppm/h on a 50 H, 500 A magnet corresponds to a total circuit resistance near 1.4 nano-ohm
facts.note: That resistance budget is why the persistent joints and the persistent current switch are the highest-risk items in the magnet, and why a magnet with a degraded joint drifts out of shim between QA sessions.

facts.label: Why helium and not something cheaper
facts.value: Helium boils at 4.222 K at 1 atm, liquid density 125 kg/m3, latent heat 20.9 kJ/kg = 2.6 kJ/L. Nitrogen boils at 77.4 K, 807 kg/m3, 199 kJ/kg = 161 kJ/L. One watt of heat leak boils 1.4 L of liquid helium per hour but only 22 mL of liquid nitrogen per hour
facts.note: Helium is the only fluid liquid at 4.2 K and it is a poor heat sink, roughly 60-fold worse per litre than nitrogen, so cryostat heat leak has to be held to a fraction of a watt rather than merely being small.

facts.label: Helium inventory, boil-off and sealed magnets
facts.value: A classic bath-cooled clinical magnet holds 1500 to 2000 L of liquid helium. With a two-stage 4 K cryocooler recondensing the vapour (typically 1.0 to 1.5 W at 4.2 K plus 30 to 50 W at 40 to 50 K, drawing 6 to 12 kW at the compressor) net boil-off is nominally zero. Sealed low-cryogen 1.5 T magnets run on about 7 L, under 0.5 percent of the classic inventory
facts.note: Zero boil-off is conditional on mains power and cooling water: lose the compressor and the magnet reverts to a plain bath cryostat boiling at its heat-leak rate, which is why the cold head belongs on emergency power in a well-built suite.

facts.label: Quench: the volume problem
facts.value: One litre of liquid helium becomes roughly 700 to 760 L of gas at room temperature and 1 atm, so a 1500 L inventory is over 1000 m3 of gas. Air is 20.9 percent oxygen; 19.5 percent is the conventional oxygen-deficient threshold, below about 16 percent gives impairment and below 10 percent rapid loss of consciousness
facts.note: The quench pipe exists to put that gas outside the building; helium is buoyant and collects at the ceiling, so an undersized, blocked or iced quench line vents into the magnet room and the hazard is asphyxiation plus a door forced shut by overpressure.

facts.label: Radiation shields and the nitrogen stage
facts.value: Radiative heat load scales as T^4, so a 77 K intermediate shield intercepts about 230-fold of the load from a 300 K wall. Liquid nitrogen expands about 1:694 at room temperature. Modern magnets replace the LN2 shield with the cryocooler first stage at 40 to 50 K
facts.note: Removing the nitrogen vessel removed a weekly fill and a second asphyxiant from the room, but it made the magnet wholly dependent on the cold head.

facts.label: NdFeB, and the Halbach point-of-care systems built from it
facts.value: Nd2Fe14B sintered grades: Br 1.0 to 1.45 T, (BH)max 200 to 470 kJ/m3 (25 to 59 MGOe), Curie temperature 310 to 400 C, usable to 80 C for plain N grades and 200 to 230 C for Dy-substituted high-coercivity grades. Reversible temperature coefficient of Br is -0.09 to -0.12 percent per K. Sparse NdFeB Halbach head scanners run at 50 to 80 mT, weigh roughly 350 to 750 kg, and reach 250 to 500 ppm homogeneity after shimming
facts.note: -0.12 percent per K is 1200 ppm per K, so a 1 K room excursion shifts B0 by about 15 kHz at 0.3 T and about 3 kHz at 64 mT; a Halbach array also cancels its own external field, which is what removes the iron return yoke and makes the system wheelable with a 5 gauss line only about 1 to 1.5 m across.

facts.label: SmCo permanent magnets
facts.value: SmCo5 and Sm2Co17: Br 0.85 to 1.15 T, (BH)max 120 to 240 kJ/m3 (16 to 32 MGOe), Curie temperature 720 C (1:5) to 800 to 850 C (2:17), usable to 300 to 350 C. Reversible temperature coefficient of Br is -0.03 to -0.05 percent per K
facts.note: You give up roughly half the energy product to gain a factor of three or four in thermal stability and intrinsic corrosion resistance, which is the trade when the magnet cannot be held at constant temperature.

facts.label: Iron: yokes, pole pieces and shim steel
facts.value: Low-carbon soft iron saturates near 2.15 T, 3 percent silicon steel near 2.0 T. Passive shimming with small steel shims in bore trays brings a 40 to 50 cm DSV from tens of ppm as wound to of order 1 ppm peak-to-peak
facts.note: Shim steel works by being magnetised by B0, so its contribution is nonlinear once it approaches saturation and it must be magnetically soft and low-remanence; a piece of hardened or cold-worked steel left in the bore behaves nothing like a shim.

facts.label: Conductors: conductivity, RF skin depth, and conductivity per kilogram
facts.value: At 20 C, silver 6.30e7 S/m (106 percent IACS), copper 5.96e7 S/m (100 percent), gold 4.10e7 S/m (70 percent), aluminium 3.77e7 S/m (61 percent). Copper skin depth is 8.2 um at 63.9 MHz (1.5 T), 5.8 um at 127.7 MHz (3 T) and 3.8 um at 298 MHz (7 T); aluminium is 10.3 um at 63.9 MHz. Aluminium carries about 2.1 times copper's conductivity per unit mass (2.70 versus 8.96 g/cm3)
facts.note: All the RF current is in the outer few microns, so a 5 to 10 um silver plating carries essentially the whole of it; silver's own 3 percent advantage in surface resistance matters far less than the fact that silver oxide still conducts while copper oxide does not, gold is reserved for contacts where zero oxide growth beats its 45 percent higher resistivity, and aluminium's mass advantage is why screens, shields and gradient formers are aluminium while the windings stay copper.

facts.label: Gradient coils: current, voltage and heat
facts.value: Clinical whole-body gradients deliver 33 to 80 mT/m at 120 to 200 T/m/s; research and head-only systems reach 300 mT/m and beyond. Amplifiers supply peak currents of 300 to 900 A (up to about 1500 A on premium systems) at 1200 to 2300 V, so peak power per axis is of order 1 MW, with mean dissipation of tens of kW removed by a chilled water loop. Internal coil temperatures reach 55 to 60 C
facts.note: Copper resistivity rises 0.39 percent per K, so a hot gradient coil needs more voltage for the same slew and the system derates; EPI and high-b diffusion are the thermal worst case and are what trips the duty-cycle interlock.

facts.label: Fringe-field shielding, the RF cage, and lead next door
facts.value: Mu-metal (approximately 77 Ni, 16 Fe, 5 Cu, 2 Mo) has relative permeability of 10^4 to 5x10^5 but saturates at only 0.74 to 0.8 T; silicon steel saturates near 2.0 T. Active shielding pulls the 5 gauss (0.5 mT) line of a 1.5 T magnet in to roughly 2.5 to 4 m, against 4 to 10 m unshielded. The RF cage is 0.1 to 0.2 mm copper sheet or 0.5 to 1.5 mm aluminium, specified at 90 to 100+ dB at the Larmor frequency. Adjoining X-ray and interventional rooms are specified at 1.6 to 3.2 mm lead equivalent, and lead conducts at only about 8 percent IACS
facts.note: Mu-metal saturates far too low to contain a scanner fringe field, so bulk passive shielding is silicon steel by the tonne; the cage needs every penetration filtered and a single-point ground because one unfiltered cable leaks more than the whole wall, and lead is an X-ray attenuator and a poor RF shield, so in a combined suite the lead and copper layers are separate and both must be continuous.

practice: Read the helium level and the cold-head runtime on every QA session, not just when something looks wrong. On a recondensing magnet a level that has started to fall is a compressor or cold-head fault, and you have days to weeks of margin, not hours.

After any cryogen work, ramp, or service that opened the bore, re-run passive and active shim and re-measure the linewidth on a phantom before you trust spectroscopy data. Shim iron trays and their fixings are frequently disturbed.

If your protocol is heavy EPI or high-b diffusion, expect the gradient duty-cycle interlock and not SAR to be the binding limit. Spread the heavy sequences through the session rather than back to back, and check whether TR or slice count can be traded before you accept a derated slew.

Treat the oxygen monitor in the magnet room as a live interlock, not a wall decoration. Check that its calibration is in date and that the room ventilation interlock actually starts, because it is the only instrument that will tell you a slow cryogen leak is happening.

On permanent-magnet and Halbach low-field systems, log room temperature with the data. A 1 K drift is 1200 ppm at -0.12 percent per K, which is a larger frequency excursion than anything you are trying to measure, and it will show up as apparent drift, line broadening or a failed frequency lock.

When specifying a new RF coil or repairing an old one, keep the silver plating at least 3 skin depths thick at the lowest Larmor frequency the coil will see (roughly 25 um covers down to 1.5 T) and do not clean plated surfaces with abrasives.

Before installing anything in the magnet room, check it against the 5 gauss line drawing for your specific magnet, not a generic one. Actively and passively shielded magnets of the same field strength differ by a factor of two or more in fringe-field extent.
pitfalls: Assuming zero boil-off means no helium risk. The cryocooler is an active machine on mains power and cooling water; if it stops, the magnet becomes an ordinary bath cryostat boiling at its heat-leak rate, and the clock to a quench starts immediately.

Quench-venting into the magnet room. A quench pipe that is undersized, corroded, obstructed by a bird's nest, or iced at the outlet will back-pressure into the room; over 1000 m3 of buoyant helium from a full inventory strips oxygen from the ceiling down and can pressure-seal the door.

Pressing the emergency field shutdown button when you mean the RF or table stop. On a bath-cooled magnet that is a deliberate quench: the helium, days of downtime, a ramp, a full reshim, and a nonzero chance of permanent coil damage. On a sealed low-cryogen magnet it is a controlled ramp-down instead, a very different cost, so know which one you have.

Using mu-metal to shield against scanner fringe field. It saturates below 0.8 T and, once saturated, is transparent; worse, forming, drilling or dropping mu-metal destroys the annealed grain structure and it has to be hydrogen-annealed again to recover its permeability.

Treating oxidised copper RF surfaces as cosmetic. Copper oxide is essentially an insulator, so a tarnished solder joint or a corroded coil element raises surface resistance and directly costs coil Q and SNR, which is exactly the failure that silver plating and gold-flashed contacts exist to prevent.

Ignoring the corrosion behaviour of NdFeB. It oxidises readily and depends on a Ni-Cu-Ni or epoxy coating; a chipped magnet block in a permanent-magnet or Halbach system loses remanence locally and puts a fixed, non-shimmable distortion into the field map.
